book: 064 - The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away

chapters.file: ch120 - In Her Glass was a Bleeding Man.md
chapters.relation: This section sets the Stones' marriages beside Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir's fifty-year open 'pact', contrasting Charlie Watts's monogamy with Jagger's wandering. Sartre and Beauvoir refused religious or social templates and defined their own rules: 'contingent' love affairs permitted, provided each told the other everything. Even this pact of honesty had casualties — lies told to their other lovers, abortions, stolen partners — so the existentialist point is that self-authored relationships trade the guilt of broken monogamy for another kind of tension.

chapters.file: ch121 - Get What You Need.md
chapters.relation: The chapter closes by matching each man's relationship style to what he 'needs': Watts keeps the beat (literally knocking Jagger out for phoning 'Where's my drummer?'), Jagger gets serial seduction, Richards trades the Anita Pallenberg cauldron for Patti Hansen's steadying presence, while Sartre died in 1980 surrounded by quarreling lovers instead of family. Every arrangement, from an Okie widow's 'plate of shit you can deal with' to the Sartre-Beauvoir pact, involves trade-offs, and the existentialist lesson is that we remain responsible for whichever romantic path we choose. Heraclitus's dictum that life is tension, and Sartre's nausea at our own choices, frame both monogamy and the pact as equally legitimate gambits.

chapters.file: ch122 - Chapter 14 - Riding the Devil’s Tank and Complicit in His Mayhem.md
chapters.relation: James Rocha opens Chapter 14 with Richards's 1971 remark that 'Everybody's Lucifer' and a mock-confession: his perfectly legal iTunes purchases of Stones records may, downstream, help finance cartel assassinations. He locates complicity in 'that mysterious gap between guilt and innocence' — you cannot be responsible for what other people do, yet you may still support, aid, or fail to stop their crimes. The chapter promises that 'Sympathy for the Devil' is the song that explains this strange concept.

chapters.file: ch123 - Philosophy by Satanic Example.md
chapters.relation: Reading 'Sympathy for the Devil' itself, the section argues the song implies an ethical position on complicity rather than devil-worship. Through an invented adultery case (Anita, Keith, and 'Mick'), it shows accountability is not a zero-sum game — one wrongful act can total 220 percent responsibility — so Lucifer, one hundred percent responsible for the evils he confesses, can still turn around and implicate 'you and me' in them.

chapters.file: ch124 - Please Allow Me to Introduce Complicity.md
chapters.relation: The section distinguishes three kinds of complicity: aiding and abetting (the groupie who took Keith Richards's driving test), membership in a collectively wrongdoing group (a state majority voting to ban the Stones), and the hybrid case — individual evil requiring mass support or inactivity. It applies the third to Altamont, where the Hell's Angels killed Meredith Hunter amid a feral atmosphere of drugs, paranoia, and three hundred thousand spectators no single one of whom is 'responsible', and to the drug wars, which persist only because users and ordinary spenders each play a small part.

chapters.file: ch125 - Killing the Kennedys—What’s Your Alibi.md
chapters.relation: The section wrestles with the song's line 'I shouted out: Who killed the Kennedys? When after all It was you and me.' Since the author has an airtight alibi — he was not alive in 1963 or 1968 — the literal reading fails, so he proposes the Kennedys as the symbol of Camelot, the utopian promise of the 1960s. On that reading our failure to protect what they stood for, from Vietnam to the later wars, is our collective complicity in their metaphorical deaths.

chapters.file: ch126 - Washing the Evil off Your Hands.md
chapters.relation: Pilate's hand-washing — 'Made damn sure that Pilate Washed his hands' — serves here as the emblem of the complicity skeptic: the thought that once responsibility fixes on someone else, everyone else's hands are clean. Noting that the ambiguous pronoun in 'washed his hands and sealed his fate' grammatically points at Pilate himself, the section argues Pilate stays complicit precisely because he permitted the execution, just as the author remains implicated in the drug wars by doing nothing to stop them.

chapters.file: ch127 - The Stench of War.md
chapters.relation: Complicity is tested against the Iraq and Afghanistan wars: the author voted against Bush and protested as much of a 'street fighting man' as he could, yet may still be complicit through taxes, votes, bumper stickers, or mere failure to speak out. He then voices the skeptic's strongest reply — that one person's inaction can hardly 'allow' a war, since stopping a war takes as much collective action as waging one — conceding that complicity here begins to look 'rather harsh'.

chapters.file: ch128 - The Puzzling Nature of the Complicity Game.md
chapters.relation: The section defends keeping complicity on two grounds: it names something real between innocence and responsibility (were Keef's drug runners responsible, complicit, or both?), and it is practically needed to shame people out of tiny roles in grave wrongs. From the song's 'kings and queens fought for ten decades for the gods they made' it draws the point that while leaders bear responsibility for war, no war effort succeeds without popular support — and zero multiplied a million times never adds up to a war, so the small contributions must be real to begin with.

chapters.file: ch129 - Restraining Lucifer with Some Courtesy, Sympathy, and Taste.md
chapters.relation: The section reads 'Just as every cop is a criminal... I'm in need of some restraint' as Lucifer speaking for the collective evil our small complicities create. The song's own solution comes in the next stanza: 'have some courtesy, have some sympathy, and some taste' become the tools for discerning our everyday contributions to large wrongs and fighting them, since if we do not, 'Lucifer really will lay our souls to waste'. On this reading 'Sympathy for the Devil' is politically deeper than critics who dismiss the Stones as hedonists will allow.

chapters.file: ch130 - Chapter 15 - The Most Dangerous Rock’n’Roll Band in the World.md
chapters.relation: Seth Vannatta opens Chapter 15 with Keith Richards's July 4th, 1975 stop at the 4-Dice restaurant in Fordyce, Arkansas, where forty minutes in the toilet getting high ended in a pull-over of a car stuffed with coke, grass, peyote, mescaline, and corn whiskey. Yet the police charged only a concealed hunting knife and 'reckless driving' from spun gravel, having tipped off the wire services in advance. The puzzle of these trumped-up charges sets up the chapter's real questions: what is law, and what exactly was rock's 'sin'?

chapters.file: ch131 - What’s the Law against Rock and Roll.md
chapters.relation: The section argues the arrest was never about the drugs: rock's 'original sin' is sex, from the term's origin as slang for sex through Elvis's censored hips and the Beatles' fainting crowds, so Arkansas's attempt to legislate rock out of existence was, the author quips, an attempt to outlaw horniness. Richards's own account of 'open season on the Stones' casts the band as suffering an extirpation 'befitting Socrates, another famous corruptor of the youth' — the state treating a mere band as a criminal corrupting force.

chapters.file: ch132 - Muddy Water and Brown Sugar.md
chapters.relation: This section digs to the deeper sin: race. Rock was born of 'race music' and the collision of white country with black gospel and blues, and it desegregated southern dance floors separated by a rope, breaking Jim Crow in practice — as the White Citizens' Council quotes the section reproduces confirm. The Stones, white but foreign, worshipping Muddy Waters, at home in black juke joints yet harassed at white truck stops, embodied the South's fear of integration and miscegenation by selling 'Brown Sugar' to white girls, and capped that stance with 'Sweet Black Angel', their solidarity song for the imprisoned Angela Davis.

chapters.file: ch133 - Keith Richards the Prophet.md
chapters.relation: The arrest becomes legal philosophy: since statutes like 'reckless driving' are general while conduct is specific, law requires the art of judgment. Against John Austin's positivism (law as the sovereign's command backed by sanction), it adopts Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.'s 'bad man' view — law is just the prediction of what courts will in fact do — making Richards a 'prophet' of consequences, as when the band declined to raise a giant inflatable phallus in San Antonio. It closes with pragmatist accounts, Holmes's law as the 'external deposit' of our moral life and Dewey's law rooted in custom and judicial behavior, explaining why the South's history of racism and sexual anxiety seeped into Arkansas law.

chapters.file: ch134 - Judge Richards Presides.md
chapters.relation: The farcical Fordyce proceeding — a golf-drunk judge sipping bourbon hidden in his sock, a BBC interview mid-trial, and Richards himself pounding the gavel at the press conference ('Case closed') — confirms for the author that Holmes was right: law is prediction all the way down, at every level from the bad man to the judge. It concludes that the 'devil' of rock was a projection of white southern fear and repressed libido, externally deposited in law yet too indeterminate to predict, as the Stones' motorcade escape at 2 a.m. showed.

chapters.file: ch135 - Chapter 16 - How Come You’re So Wrong, My Sweet Neo Con.md
chapters.relation: Joseph Foy introduces 'Sweet Neo Con' from A Bigger Bang (2005) as the Stones' most direct political statement — Jagger's blunt, non-metaphorical attack on Bush-era Christian hypocrisy, phony patriotism, and corporatist cronyism. Noting that the left (Michael Moore, Bill Moyers) cheered while the right (Matt Drudge) called it geriatric pandering, he argues both sides misread the song, which actually crystallizes the band's lifelong role in defining the public sphere.

chapters.file: ch136 - No Place for a Street Fighting Man.md
chapters.relation: This section explains why the Stones seem apolitical beside Lennon's bed-ins and Dylan's protest songs: they rarely joined overt activism, and 'Street Fighting Man' remained only a hint. It then argues the judgment rests on too narrow a conception of the public sphere — the space connecting state and private life — because by legitimizing an anti-establishment counter-cultural identity and pushing rebellion into the mainstream (capped by the SS-uniform protest after Ed Sullivan censored 'Let's Spend the Night Together'), the Stones did political work without electoral politics.

chapters.file: ch137 - Like a Rollin’ Stone.md
chapters.relation: Building the strong/weak publics distinction — rally-goers pursue decisions, concert-goers form identity — the section argues the Stones' influence runs through 'political socialization': prolonged emotional attachment to a rebellious worldview, from the tongue logo on dorm walls to 'Satisfaction's' indictment of mainstream media, gradually makes fans more distrustful of centralized power and state enforcement of cultural agendas. That slow identity shift, not candidate endorsement, is their politics.

chapters.file: ch138 - My Sweet Neo Con.md
chapters.relation: This section reconstructs neo-conservatism from Daniel Bell and Irving Kristol — ex-radicals disillusioned by Stalinism who, unlike traditional conservatives, would wield state power to restore traditional values — as the precise opposite of the Stones' licentious image, with Altamont's killing of Meredith Hunter cited as the movement's stock exhibit. It quotes Allan Bloom's portrait of Jagger as a 'shrewd, middle-class boy' playing the possessed demon while winking at the money-handlers, and Robert Bork's Slouching Towards Gomorrah: the neo-con fear that if Jagger is happily 'beyond the law', so is every one of his fans.

chapters.file: ch139 - Oh No, Not You Again.md
chapters.relation: The section details 'Sweet Neo Con's' specific targets: Pentagon money over social programs, profiteering by Halliburton and KBR, unilateral regime-change warfare, and Eisenhower's revived 'military-industrial complex' — so scathing that Richards, living in the United States, worried about audience blowback. Its thesis is that the song breaks nothing new: it merely makes overt the anti-authority battle lines the band had always drawn covertly.

chapters.file: ch140 - If You Turn Out Right, I’ll Eat My Hat Tonight.md
chapters.relation: The short closing section argues that in the mass-media age the line between political message and private life has dissolved: 'nearly all activities are now political', so sorting public-sphere discourse from private identity formation no longer tracks anything real. The Stones' covert 1960s rebellion and the overt 'Sweet Neo Con' are therefore one continuous project of resisting the single social mold neo-conservatives tried to impose — and Foy bets it will not be the last confrontation.

chapters.file: ch141 - Chapter 17 - Keef for President.md
ch142 - My Name Is Called Disturbance.md
chapters.relation: This section auditions Keith for the presidency by separating the actor's art — Reagan, Ventura, and Franken winning office by expertly provoking audiences' emotions — from the musician's. Keith's creativity runs the other way: a private 'aesthetic conversation' with his own soul and the muses rather than empathy for a character, which is why his music is believable where actors' albums fail. Whether he should be president thus turns on what values that refined instinct about 'the good' would supply in a leader.

chapters.file: ch143 - A Palace Revolution.md
chapters.relation: The fantasy election brings in Plato's Republic: Richards's defense attorney Bill Carter functions as his Ring of Gyges, letting him vanish from legal consequences and raising Plato's question of whether we act justly only from fear of punishment. The tripartite soul is mapped onto Keef — appetites (drugs, sex, Jagger's 'Bitch'), spirit (the Glimmer Twins' rivalry), rationality (busting his head reaching for a library book) — and justice becomes the harmony under rationality's rule. In the ideal city of philosopher kings, auxiliaries, and workers, the sign at the gate reads 'NO POETS, NO ROCK'N'ROLLERS': Richards is exactly the corrupting poet Plato bars.

chapters.file: ch144 - Shout and Scream and Kill the King.md
chapters.relation: The election plays out: Richards blows away the auxiliaries with 'Play with Fire' and whips the working-class appetites into a frenzy (put on Exile on Main Street after a few rounds to test Plato's fear of the poets). Young Keef's soul is appetite-led — the 'Blue Lena' Bentley with its hidden drug compartment embodies a spirit in service of drugs and artistic hunger, with rationality demoted to scoring the fix. The resulting Republic of Keef, driven fast on the edge of a cliff, vindicates Plato's warning that wherever the appetites lead, tyranny soon follows — as the author concedes through his own pipe-smoking.

chapters.file: ch145 - Compromise Solution.md
chapters.relation: This section pushes back on Plato: the author has never met anyone as harmonious as the just man and calls the philosopher king 'a fairytale'. Quoting Republic Book VIII's portrait of the democratic soul that 'lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour', he concedes the description fits his own life and polity — yet insists that a life without good sex, good food, and good conversation would be 'bereft of serious value', which sets up the book's compromise.

chapters.file: ch146 - What Can a Poor Boy Do, but Sing in a Rock’n’Roll Band.md
chapters.relation: The finale concedes Plato's point that justice involves self-control — enough to make a voter pause at the sexual appetites of JFK and Bill Clinton — while refusing the ascetic cure and the President-Keith ticket. The author decides he could not live under Keef's rule but wants him permanently at the edge of town, playing a juke joint: a spirit worth tuning into as a reminder that control is 'ultimately an illusion', visited on midnight rides and returned from before morning comes.

chapters.file: ch147 - V - Undercover of the Knight.md
ch148 - Chapter 18 - Sympathy for The Stones.md
ch149 - Killing One “Traditional” Bird with Five Stones.md
ch150 - The Devil Went Down to Altamont.md
chapters.relation: This chapter-opening section recounts how 'Sympathy for the Devil' tauntingly catalogs historical horrors — Christ's passion, the Romanovs, the Holocaust, the Kennedys, the Hundred Years War — over a samba rhythm, and how violence broke out at Altamont as it was performed, leaving four dead including Meredith Hunter (stabbed during 'Under My Thumb'). It argues the satanic label misses the point: the lyrics are really 'a rough sketch of virtue and a call for societal compassion', the kind of reorientation of the soul — a periagoge — that befitted even St. Augustine.

chapters.file: ch151 - What Happens in Carthage Stays in Carthage.md
chapters.relation: The section likens Augustine's adolescence in Carthage — the Las Vegas of his day — to a rolling-stone youth of sex and sin, noting that Jagger was actually the more responsible teen, enrolling at the London School of Economics. Its key move: in the song's catalog of atrocities the Devil only watches ('I watched with glee') and never causes, so if Lucifer is not the guilty party, the evil must be human — exactly the question Augustine's Confessions was written to answer.

chapters.file: ch152 - (I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction . . . Or the Satisfaction that I Ought To.md
chapters.relation: Augustine's theory of evil is explained through a concert-photography analogy: a dark photo of a brightly lit stage contains no real darkness, just a camera lacking proper exposure, fixable with editing. Likewise, evil is not an entity or polar opposite of good but a privation — something missing the 'good-making' features it ought to have — so no Devil is needed to explain the darkness in the world or in us.

chapters.file: ch153 - Who’s to Blame.md
chapters.relation: The section turns to Augustine's pear theft, where 'it was the sin that sweetened' the act: evil is chosen for the thrill of the forbidden, not forced by any demonic power. It names this 'moral impotence' — knowing the right yet willingly choosing the wrong, as with a missed curfew — an instinct no era has cured. The background vocals' 'Who? Who?' and Jagger's 'I'll tell you one time, you're to blame' thus land the blame for history's catastrophes squarely on 'you and me'.

chapters.file: ch154 - Sympathy for The Stones.md
chapters.relation: This section stages the Stones' defense as a rerun of Socrates' trial in the Apology, charge by charge: atheism (deflected by the song's own invocation of Lucifer and of right and wrong), sophistry (the Stones were not in it for money in the 1960s, as Socrates took no fees and lived poor), and corrupting the youth (Socrates never sought his crowds — they found him, just as fans camped out for Stones tickets). Like Socrates, who accepted his death sentence while Athens committed 'the great sin against philosophy', the band was exiled to the south of France rather than back down, and music was the better for its refusal.

chapters.file: ch155 - Chapter 19 - How Mick Learned to Love the Devil.md
chapters.relation: Richard Berger opens Chapter 19 with the biographical key to 'Sympathy for the Devil': Marianne Faithfull gave Jagger Mikhail Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita during their relationship, and the song — along with 'Sister Morphine' and 'Wild Horses' — grew from that literary influence. The novel is itself a critique of Saint Augustine's philosophy of evil, which makes 'Sympathy' a very moral song: a response to and updating of Augustine rather than a hymn to black magic.

chapters.file: ch156 - Just as Every Cop Is a Criminal, and All the Sinners Saints.md
chapters.relation: This section lays out Augustine's journey from the Manichean two-gods heresy, through reading Plato, to the view of evil as an 'absence' rather than a force. Its core is the dilemma of Confessions 7.3: if God is wholly good, who sowed the 'seed of bitterness' — the wicked will — into us, and who made the devil? Augustine's answer runs through original sin (the pride of Adam and Eve, demons as fallen angels) and an awkward compromise on which humans are free yet constrained by predestination, so that evil becomes necessary — and confession itself a good.

chapters.file: ch157 - Please Allow Me to Introduce Myself.md
chapters.relation: The section tells how Bulgakov's novel, begun in 1928, stifled by Stalin, and published in English only in 1967, reached Jagger through Faithfull in 1968. It summarizes the opening: Satan disguised as Professor Woland interrupts two Moscow atheists, savages the literary elite's vanity and secularism, and argues in explicitly Augustinian, predestinarian terms that man cannot even vouch for his own tomorrow — in a Russia so Godless it takes the Devil himself to restore belief, since everyone, Devil included, is part of the divine plan.

chapters.file: ch158 - And I Was ’Round when Jesus Christ Had His Moment of Doubt and Pain.md
chapters.relation: This section follows the novel-within-the-novel — the Master's gospel of Yeshua Ha-Nozri before a reluctant Pilate, with Matthew the Levite embellishing the miracles — and its frame: Margarita's masked ball of the risen dead, Berlioz's talking severed head, and God's final order to Woland granting the lovers peace and forgiving even Pilate. Bulgakov thus agrees with Augustine that evil exists yet all of us carry good that can unite with the Divine by turning from the material world; his Satan, operating 'like an employee of a large organization' inside God's constraints, is why we naturally have sympathy for this Devil.

chapters.file: ch159 - But What’s Puzzling You Is the Nature of My Game.md
chapters.relation: The section situates the song after the 1967 Redlands Bust and amid 1968's collapses — Paris riots, Vietnam, Bobby Kennedy's assassination, which forced the lyric change from 'Who killed Kennedy?' to 'Who killed the Kennedys?' the night before a recording session. Against both Augustine and Bulgakov, it argues Jagger's Devil is far more human and unpredestined: by demanding we 'guess my name', the song fingers us as Satan, tracing the world's malice to our own impulses rather than any divinely scripted plan.

chapters.file: ch160 - I Tell You One Time, You’re to Blame.md
chapters.relation: The closing section follows the song's aftermath through Godard's session film — Brian Jones inaudible in his booth as a Dylanesque draft turns into a 'rocking samba' — to Jones's death, the Altamont killing (shown by Gimme Shelter to have happened during 'Under My Thumb', not 'Sympathy'), and the end of Mick and Marianne. Its verdict: Augustine's narrow, predestined free will leaves humanity out of the picture, while Jagger's human Devil puts responsibility back on us — a world without the Stones would be less enlightened about evil, and their song 'demands more of us, perhaps, than Augustine's Confessions'.

holes.name: Complicity
holes.what: Accountability short of guilt for wrongdoing that one supports, enables, or fails to prevent, including collective complicity dispersed across millions of small contributions.
holes.why: All of Chapter 14 (ch122-129) is built on complicity as the concept 'between guilt and innocence', and taxonomy has no slug for it.

holes.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.
holes.what: American jurist and legal pragmatist who defined law, from the 'bad man's' perspective, as a prediction of what the courts will in fact do.
holes.why: Ch133-134 explain Richards's Fordyce arrest and drunken trial through Holmes's prediction theory of law.

holes.name: John Austin
holes.what: Legal positivist who defined law as the command of a political superior imposing a duty, backed by a sanction for disobedience.
holes.why: Ch133 uses Austin's command theory as the positivist foil against which Holmes's bad-man realism is defended.

holes.name: Legal Realism (law as prediction)
holes.what: The view that law is not a self-contained logical system of statutes but a prediction of judicial behavior, indeterminate and rooted in custom and social practice.
holes.why: Ch133-134 apply exactly this view to Richards's arrest, making the band's lawyer-and-judge antics the test case for what law is.

holes.name: Allan Bloom
holes.what: Conservative philosopher who in The Closing of the American Mind attacked rock music and popular culture as debasing the young without authentic political content.
holes.why: Ch138 quotes Bloom's portrait of Jagger at length as the philosophical case that rock rebellion is merely commercial envy of money and fame.

holes.name: Neo-conservatism
holes.what: Movement (Bell, Kristol) of disillusioned liberals willing to use state power to restore traditional order against 1960s liberalism, the counterculture, and bands like the Stones.
holes.why: Chapter 16 (ch135-140) frames 'Sweet Neo Con' and the band's whole political identity as a collision with neo-conservatism, which taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Mikhail Bulgakov
holes.what: Russian novelist whose The Master and Margarita stages a sympathetic, Augustinian Devil (Woland) working within God's plan in an atheistic Moscow.
holes.why: Chapter 19 (ch155-160) reads 'Sympathy for the Devil' as Jagger's response to Bulgakov's novel and its critique of Augustine's notion of evil.
